title: Round 15 - three accounts, three scoring bases
focus: Does the funding shape of an account change which strategy belongs in it? Fourteen rounds had only ever scored one kind of account - a taxable lump sum with no contributions - because that was all the engine could express. All 54 scored agents across every committed round are trading-purpose cards. Round 15 opens the savings and Roth arms for the first time, which meant building a bridge before it could ask anything at all.
headline: Funding shape changes the answer, in the opposite direction to the one predicted: the monthly drip lost to an equivalent lump sum in two of three windows, winning only in the one containing a bear market.
outcome:
The round had to build its own instrument first. Allocation and ladder results are separate pydantic models from AgentResult, so the scorer could not load a single round-15 candidate; capital_exposure means a different quantity for a rebalanced book than for a stock picker, so the programme's primary rank key silently becomes a different metric when fed one; and the only harness that models a deposit stream or computes an IRR takes a hand-written function rather than a card. Two adapters closed that: a ScoredRun reader that refuses to produce an adjusted_excess for an invested-value basis rather than warning about it, and a card_weight_fn that lets one frozen card run both lump-sum through the engine and contribution-funded through the harness.

The bridge was gated before it was trusted, and the two gates disagree in an informative way. On target weights it is exact - 753 comparisons, zero mismatches, worst gap zero. On ending equity the two paths sit 0.66% apart, and the cause is not the bridge: the engine drives a real cash account and rejected 58 buy orders it could not fund, while the contribution harness has no cash constraint and always rebalances to target. So every savings and Roth figure in this round is systematically optimistic, most so in exactly the case that matters - a deep drawdown in a leveraged sleeve, when rebalancing is most valuable and least affordable. That caveat is stamped on every record as cash_constraint_modelled: false rather than left in a document.

Of four pre-registered predictions, three held and one was falsified. The falsified one is the most useful. Predicting that a monthly drip would favour the most volatile card, the reasoning was that a drip buys more of a sleeve that has fallen. Run against an equivalent lump sum through the same harness - only the timing of the money differing - the drip lost by 2.78 points in h10y-1 and 0.80 in h10y-2, and won by 2.52 only in h5y-3, the single window containing a bear market. The mechanism was real and visible; it just is not the dominant term. Across a rising decade, the cost of being out of the market swamps the benefit of buying its dips.

What held: IRR and time-weighted CAGR diverged by more than two points on exactly one card, and it was the one holding 35% in a 2x-leveraged sleeve (3.11pp, against 1.86 and below for everything else) - which is why the protocol requires both figures and not the flattering one. Drip size moved magnitudes but never the ordering, at $500 and $1,000 across three windows. And nothing beat QQQ on both return and drawdown, and a same-day correction by round 16 strengthened that: ladder-sso-vig-bnd's figures here were contaminated by a stateful ladder closure reused across windows, and corrected it never beat QQQ on either return or drawdown in any window -- see this round's SELECTION.md correction of 2026-08-24.

On whether conditional tilts earn their complexity, asked three times with matched pairs on identical sleeves: in the Roth arm, yes - the mean-reversion variant beat its static twin in 5 of 5 windows for about 1.5 points of extra drawdown. In the trading arm it depends entirely on regime - the ATR tilt was worth +3.65 points in the GFC and cost 2.15 in COVID, and in the 'recent' window it was identical to its static twin to the last decimal, because the gate never fired once in a full year.

Two cards could not be measured, and both are reported rather than worked around. spy-schd-agg-gld-bil-atr-tilt cannot run in the savings arm at all: its rules gate on atr(14), ATR needs high and low, and the contribution harness passes closes only. Letting the tilts silently never fire would have scored it as its own static twin and answered the round's central question with a number containing no tilts. And qld-schd-sgov is unranked in two of five long windows because SGOV's bars begin 2020-06-01 - a data-coverage fact, not a verdict on the strategy.
carries_forward: A LadderCard's card_weight_fn closure is a STATE MACHINE (armed rung depth, cycle-starting high); an AllocationCard's is stateless. Build a fresh closure per cell, never one reused across windows -- round 15 reused one and contaminated every ladder window after the first, by up to 16 points of CAGR. The first window is always correct, which is exactly what makes the defect hard to see.

Every contribution-funded number carries an unmeasured optimistic bias, because contributions.simulate has no cash constraint while the real engine rejects unfundable buys. Running the contribution arms through a cash-aware broker is the highest-value follow-up, and it may specifically move the P1 result - the drip's only win is in h5y-3, the bear-market window, which is exactly where a real account would most often fail to fund the rebalance it is being credited for.

Do not read a savings or Roth figure against a trading figure. They are IRR and time-weighted CAGR against adjusted_excess, and the ScoredRun reader now raises rather than producing an adjusted_excess for an invested-value basis - that refusal is deliberate and should not be routed around with a fallback.

Nothing is promoted. PROTOCOL.md section 6 needs two consecutive rounds on differing window sets, and this is the first round any savings or Roth card has ever run in. The empty leaderboards were absence of measurement, not poor results; they are now populated and still not a basis for moving a card between tiers.

Vol-targeting and inverse-vol risk parity remain inexpressible, because TiltRule.shift_pct is a fixed Decimal rather than a function of an indicator's magnitude. ALLOCATION-FAMILY.md found the vol-target variant strongest on risk-adjusted terms and it is still not a card. Closing that needs a formula-valued tilt field or a fourth card type - a boolean staircase imitating a continuous function was explicitly refused as smuggling.
A tilt that never fires is not free. qqq-ief-gld-atr-tilt was byte-identical to its static twin across the whole 'recent' window; it still costs parameters in the budget and attention in the reading.
